analysis.one_liner: Phases out the legal subminimum wage for workers with disabilities and pays employers to move them into regular jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 25, 2025 with a bipartisan pair of sponsors and 8 cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a Depression-era provision of federal labor law, employers can get a special certificate that lets them pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage — sometimes only a few dollars an hour or less. This bill raises those wages step by step until they reach the full minimum wage within four years, then ends the certificates entirely. To ease the change, it offers federal grants ($2 million to $10 million for states, $100,000 to $500,000 for individual employers) to help disability employers convert their programs into regular, community-based jobs at normal pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are currently paid less than the minimum wage under a special certificate. Their wages would rise in steps — to 60% of the federal minimum at the start, then 70%, 80%, 90%, and the full minimum wage after four years — and they would be moved toward regular jobs in the community alongside workers without disabilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act provision that allows special certificates to pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage, raising their pay in yearly steps until it reaches the full federal minimum wage after four years [S2].
It bars the Labor Department from issuing new special certificates to any employer that did not already hold one, and sunsets all existing certificates four years after the wage phase-in begins [S2].

It creates grant programs for states ($2 million to $10 million over five years) and for certificate-holding employers ($100,000 to $500,000 over three years) to transform their business models into competitive integrated employment — regular jobs in the community at the same pay others receive for similar work [S2].
It requires annual public reporting on the wages, hours, and demographics of workers still paid under certificates, and an independent multi-year evaluation of the effects of the transition [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that hold special certificates — largely nonprofit disability service providers running segregated 'sheltered workshop' programs — would lose the ability to pay below-minimum wages and would have to pay full wages or change how they operate. Federal taxpayers would fund the grant and evaluation programs, authorized at $50 million per year through fiscal 2031.

drawbacks.text: Some workers and their families value sheltered workshop jobs, and when the certificates expire those jobs as they exist today would end; the bill's answer is to require every certificate holder to transition affected workers into competitive integrated employment, but whether enough regular jobs exist to absorb them is an open question [S2].

The transition is costly and slow: wage floors rise over four years, employers get one-time grants of at most $500,000, and the whole program is authorized at $50 million a year, which may not cover the full cost of retraining, job coaching, and wraparound services for affected workers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a legally sanctioned two-tier wage — where the same work can be paid less because the worker has a disability — would be phased out, at real transition cost to the employers that depend on it and to taxpayers who fund the conversion. The main risk to workers is not the wage increase itself but whether each worker can actually land a regular job; the bill tries to manage that risk with grant conditions, priority for people with the most significant disabilities, and mandated reporting, but the outcome will depend on execution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA) introduced the bill on July 25, 2025, joined by Rep. Pete Sessions (R-TX), and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1][S2][S4].
Eight members have cosponsored the bill, six Democrats and two Republicans; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no action taken, the employers holding 14(c) certificates continue operating under current law and can keep paying subminimum wages; workers with disabilities get no wage increase.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and other 14(c) certificate holders
industries.note: These employers — mostly nonprofit disability service providers — can currently pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage under a special certificate. The bill strips that authority, requiring them to pay at least the federal minimum and eventually ending the certificates outright.

industries.industry: Disability employment and supported-employment service providers
industries.note: States and employers converting to community-based, full-wage employment can receive federal grants of up to $10 million (states) or $500,000 (employers), plus a six-year national technical assistance contract for a nonprofit.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in committee with bipartisan sponsorship but no scheduled action. Versions of this proposal have been introduced in previous Congresses without advancing to a vote, so the likely path is that it stalls in the Education and Workforce Committee unless the chair schedules a markup — which typically only happens with a signal from leadership.
